cards.title: Reading a live playlist
cards.principle: A player discovers media through a playlist. A master playlist describes variants. A media playlist gives the segments for one rendition. A successful playlist request proves only the first step in playback.
cards.practice: Follow one variant to its media playlist. Read consecutive media sequence numbers and durations, then play across a segment boundary. Repeat on the affected device class.
cards.example: A fictional garden channel opens on a laptop but stalls on a small player. Compare the same variant and segment window before changing the encoder.
cards.check: The media sequence advances across refreshes, new segments arrive in time, and the player crosses the suspect boundary.

cards.title: Testing an adaptive switch
cards.principle: Adaptive playback changes quality as bandwidth changes. A switch can fail when two individually playable renditions disagree about timing or declared codecs.
cards.practice: Pick adjacent variants. Compare their timelines and declarations. Constrain bandwidth, allow a switch in both directions, and inspect audio continuity.
cards.example: Two invented renditions play alone. Only a downward switch repeats half a sentence. Check alignment around that cut before lowering every bitrate.
cards.check: Capture a real switch with continuous picture and sound at the same program moment in both directions.

cards.title: Finding the boundary of caption drift
cards.principle: A constant caption offset and an offset that grows over time point to different checks. The first can follow an initial timestamp error. The second calls for duration and time-base comparisons.
cards.practice: Choose an audible word near the start, middle and end. Compare cue start to speech at all three points, then repeat after a seek or discontinuity.
cards.example: In a fictional short film the first caption lands on time. By the closing line it leads the speaker. Shifting the whole file would move the opening out of sync.
cards.check: Check the same three points and a seek with captions enabled on the intended player. Confirm cues remain readable and complete.

cards.title: Verifying audio tracks
cards.principle: Visible language labels and audible media are separate parts of track selection. A correct label can still lead to the wrong rendition.
cards.practice: Compare the track label, declared language, default flags and audio group. Select each track, identify a known passage, then change quality and seek.
cards.example: An invented short offers narration on a second audio track. Its menu label is correct, but selecting it plays the main mix after a quality switch.
cards.check: A listener can select the intended track, hear its distinctive passage, and keep that selection through the transition.

cards.title: Narrowing a playback incident
cards.principle: Start with one precise symptom and a comparison that changes one variable. Record observable impact separately from a suspected cause.
cards.practice: Choose an affected item, a control item, a device class and a time window. Hold three fixed while changing the fourth. Identify the earliest boundary where results diverge.
cards.example: An invented player shows a spinner for one program. The prior program plays on the same connection. Use that contrast to narrow the next check.
cards.check: A second observer can repeat the comparison and identify which boundary still needs evidence.

cards.title: Proving a fix reached the viewer
cards.principle: A successful change request confirms the system accepted work. Recovery also requires a fresh observation from the part of the service the audience uses.
cards.practice: Save the original symptom and scope. Check the changed input, the next consumer, and a fresh viewer session. Include one unaffected control.
cards.example: A fictional catalog record is corrected at its source. An older copy still appears in the player. Check the next refresh before declaring recovery.
cards.check: The original journey succeeds from a fresh session and a control still behaves normally. Record what remains untested.

cards.title: Choosing a stop condition
cards.principle: A small release is informative when the early group sees representative traffic and a defined signal can stop further rollout.
cards.practice: Choose a viewer-facing measure, a comparable control group, a minimum observation window and an action if the measure worsens.
cards.example: A fictional player update looks healthy on menus. The early rollout excludes long playback sessions. Extend the observation before expanding exposure.
cards.check: The comparison includes the risky behavior and a second operator can use the same rule to proceed, hold or reverse.

cards.title: Writing an incident handoff
cards.principle: A handoff lets the next person act without rediscovering the symptom. Separate observations, hypotheses and the work still open.
cards.practice: Write the impact in plain language. Add the smallest reproducible check, time window, evidence location, owner role and next decision point.
cards.example: A fictional night shift finds captions missing on one rendition. Hand over the exact comparison and the pending downstream check.
cards.check: An incoming operator can run the named check and knows what finding would change the next action.

cards.title: Matching a title to the right edition
cards.principle: Similar titles can describe different works, cuts or episodes. Prefer stable identifiers within their declared namespace and use independent fields to confirm the edition.
cards.practice: Compare source identifiers, series membership, episode position, language, duration and cut. Put contradictory records into a review queue.
cards.example: Two fictional specials share a title. One is a recap and the other a full episode. Their durations differ and only one belongs in the season sequence.
cards.check: The chosen record resolves to the expected edition across both systems. Document the deciding field and preserve the alternate record.

cards.title: Reconciling conflicting runtimes
cards.principle: A schedule slot, an editorial running time and the measured media duration answer different questions. Compare fields only after identifying their definitions and units.
cards.practice: Trace each value to its source. Convert to the same unit, inspect rounding and compare against the delivered cut including credits.
cards.example: A fictional program occupies a half-hour slot. Its delivered episode ends several minutes earlier. The schedule alone cannot decide the playback runtime.
cards.check: The consumer field names the intended concept and agrees with a measured or editorially confirmed value for that cut.

cards.title: Tracing a stale field
cards.principle: When copies disagree, trace one field through each transformation. A newer timestamp may describe an import time while the field itself came from an older source.
cards.practice: Match the record identity, capture each field value and its effective timestamp, then compare the transform and refresh boundary where values first diverge.
cards.example: A fictional synopsis is correct upstream and old in search. Inspect the exported record and search refresh separately before editing the source again.
cards.check: After refresh, the same record and field agree at the intended boundaries. Preserve the evidence for the first divergence.

cards.title: Checking a schedule boundary
cards.principle: A local calendar day and a UTC interval can straddle different dates. A release also needs an explicit convention for the start and end of its window.
cards.practice: Write the intended zone, convert both endpoints, and exercise just before, exactly at and just after each edge. Include daylight-saving changes when relevant.
cards.example: A fictional evening screening crosses midnight. Its listing disappears early because a local date was interpreted as a UTC midnight.
cards.check: The listing and player agree with the intended inclusive or exclusive rule on both edges, in the audience zone.

cards.title: Checking a picture edit for continuity
cards.principle: Continuity depends on what the viewer follows. Screen direction, eyeline and the timing of an action can make two technically clean shots feel disconnected.
cards.practice: Watch the cut at normal speed without sound. Identify the point of attention in each shot, then check the motion across the cut frame by frame.
cards.example: In a fictional scene a bird reaches for a seed. The reverse angle starts with the seed already lifted. Move the cut to a shared phase of the action.
cards.check: A first-time viewer follows the gesture at normal speed. Watch again with sound to catch a newly awkward audio transition.

cards.title: Comparing loudness and peaks
cards.principle: Integrated loudness describes a whole program. True peak measures short peaks. Two mixes can share one measure and differ on the other.
cards.practice: Identify the delivery specification, measure the complete program and check true peaks. Listen to quiet speech and the loudest transition on a representative device.
cards.example: A fictional short meets its integrated target but a slammed door clips after encoding. Inspect that transient and recheck the encoded deliverable.
cards.check: The finished file meets the destination specification and dialogue stays understandable in the intended listening context.

cards.title: Making visual storytelling audible
cards.principle: When essential story information is visual, decide how a listener can learn it. Describe the action in a natural gap or build the information into the original narration.
cards.practice: Listen without looking. List the missing facts needed to follow the story, find spaces for concise descriptions, then listen again with dialogue and music.
cards.example: In a fictional scene a character hides a map without speaking. A short description in a pause explains why the search in the next scene matters.
cards.check: A listener can follow the change without guessing and the description leaves essential dialogue audible.

cards.title: Checking the exported master
cards.principle: A timeline preview and an exported file can differ. Check the same artifact that will actually be handed off and play through its risky boundaries.
cards.practice: Inspect container, picture, audio tracks, caption presence and runtime. Watch the opening, closing, scene changes and any points changed since the last export.
cards.example: A fictional master looks fine in the editor, but the final export omits its second audio track. Inspect the track inventory and play that version.
cards.check: A reviewer can identify the exact export checked, open it independently and verify the destination requirements.

cards.title: Designing a keyboard journey
cards.principle: Keyboard users need to reach each action, activate it and recover their place. An obvious visual button can still have an inaccessible name or unusable focus order.
cards.practice: Complete the main task using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space as appropriate. Check visible focus, meaningful names and where focus returns after dismissal.
cards.example: A fictional filter panel closes after a choice but focus jumps to the top. Return it to the control that opened the panel.
cards.check: The same task works without a pointer, with a visible focus indicator and a predictable next Tab stop.

cards.title: Designing a useful print view
cards.principle: Paper has fixed edges and loses interactions. A usable print view makes the document subject, reading order and essential artwork explicit.
cards.practice: Choose the intended item, hide navigation, set print margins and check page breaks on both Letter and A4. Inspect the actual preview or exported PDF.
cards.example: A fictional activity page prints its whole picker ahead of the selected sheet. Isolate the selected artwork and print its title with it.
cards.check: Each supported paper size contains the intended item with a legible title and complete artwork within printable bounds.

cards.title: Respecting a reduced-motion preference
cards.principle: Motion may communicate change, but some viewers require a quieter path. Preserve the meaning of the transition with position, text or a stable state.
cards.practice: Enable the system preference before loading the page. Navigate and update the page. Check decorative movement and any motion triggered by interaction.
cards.example: A fictional gallery slides cards on every keypress. Under reduced motion it swaps cards directly and keeps the visible selection label.
cards.check: The user completes the same task, can identify the selected item and avoids unnecessary movement under the preference.

cards.title: Designing a data-minimal feature
cards.principle: Start with the decision a feature needs to make. Every additional input creates a handling and retention obligation.
cards.practice: List required outputs and work backward to the smallest inputs. Try a local calculation before adding an upload. Check actual network and storage behavior.
cards.example: A fictional recommendation tool needs a topic choice. A session-local choice produces the same lesson without recording the visitor’s typed words.
cards.check: The feature works with only its declared inputs. Network and persistence checks agree with the interface disclosure.

cards.title: Understanding retrieval-augmented generation
cards.principle: A retrieval system selects passages and supplies them as context to an answer generator. Retrieval can improve grounding only if the passages contain the answer.
cards.practice: Trace one question through query handling, retrieval, context assembly and the answer. Inspect the selected passage before tuning the wording of a prompt.
cards.example: A fictional library guide must explain borrowing rules. Retrieving the right branch policy matters more than a confident paraphrase of an unrelated rule.
cards.check: For a known question, the supporting passage appears in context and the answer agrees with it. An unsupported question receives an explicit gap.

cards.title: Choosing lexical or semantic retrieval
cards.principle: Term matching is strong for exact codes and rare names. Embeddings can find paraphrases, but similarity alone does not establish factual relevance.
cards.practice: Build a small set of exact-match and paraphrase queries. Compare relevant passages within the same result limit, then inspect disagreements by query type.
cards.example: A fictional manual uses a short part code and a plain-language fault description. A combined search may locate both if its ranker is evaluated on both kinds of request.
cards.check: The chosen approach improves the intended query group without hiding exact identifiers on the control queries.

cards.title: Separating retrieval and answer quality
cards.principle: A fluent answer can hide a retrieval miss. Score passage selection and answer support separately, and include questions the collection cannot answer.
cards.practice: Annotate which passages can answer a small test set. Measure how often an adequate passage is retrieved, then assess claims against those passages and track abstentions.
cards.example: In a fictional FAQ, an answer picks the wrong return window even though the correct passage ranked first. Changing retrieval alone would miss the error.
cards.check: A report identifies retrieval misses, unsupported claims and incorrect abstentions separately. Repeat the same test set after a change.

cards.title: Choosing retrieval or model training
cards.principle: Retrieval changes which material a system can consult at answer time. Training changes model parameters. Different failure modes call for different experiments.
cards.practice: If facts change often, test updating a small collection. If the failure is a stable task behavior, compare instructions and examples before considering a training run.
cards.example: A fictional club changes its opening hours each season. Updating the approved source and checking its retrieval gives a direct way to inspect the current answer.
cards.check: Use held-out examples and stale-fact questions to determine which change helped. Record failures as well as improvements.
